frames.narration: 1,000 user ids arrive in random order and go into a plain binary search tree. The tree ends up with height 21 and lookups cost about 11 comparisons. Tested like this, it looks fine.

In production the ids arrive in increasing order. Each new key is larger than all earlier ones, so it hangs off the right of the last node: the tree is a chain of height 1,000, building it needs 499,500 comparisons and a lookup up to 1,000.

A self-balancing tree (AVL, red-black, or a B-tree with many keys per node) rotates after inserts. On the same sorted ids an AVL tree has height 10 and needs 8,987 comparisons for 1,000 lookups instead of 500,500. The guarantee holds for any order.
Now a graph of 100,000 places with 2 roads each. An adjacency list stores only the roads that exist: V + 2E = 500,000 cells.

An adjacency matrix has a cell for every pair of places: 100,000 x 100,000 = 10 billion cells, about 80 GB at 8 bytes each, and a search has to scan whole rows, so breadth-first search costs 10,000,100,000 steps instead of 500,000.
A breadth-first search visits each place once and looks at each road once, but only because it marks places as visited. Without that set, any cycle sends it round forever.

For weighted roads, Dijkstra's algorithm with a heap takes about (V + 2E) log V = 8,500,000 steps here. Scanning for the nearest place each round costs 10,000,400,000. And one search from the source gives every destination: 100 separate searches would cost 100 times as much.

Last trap: recursive depth-first search nests as deep as the longest path. On a graph shaped like a path of 100,000 places that is 100,000 stack frames, past the default limits of many runtimes (Python: 1,000).
